text: Nnoseng Ellen Kate Kuzwayo (29 June 1914 – 19 April 2006) was a South African women's rights activist and politician who taught from 1938 to 1952. She served as president of the African National Congress Youth League in the 1960s and was secretary of the ANC Youth League in the 1940s. In 1994, she was elected to the first post-apartheid South African Parliament at the age of 79 and served for five years until June 1999, becoming South Africa's longest-serving parliamentarian. Her autobiography, Call Me Woman (1985), won the CNA Literary Award, making her the first black writer to receive South Africa's leading literary prize. Born Nnoseng Ellen Serasengwe in Thaba 'Nchu, Orange Free State, she came from an educated, politically active family. Her maternal grandfather, Jeremaiah Makgothi, was taken to the Cape in circa 1875 to attend the Lovedale Institute, where he qualified as a teacher, worked as a court interpreter, and served as a Methodist lay preacher; he was the only layman to work with Robert Moffat on the translation of the Bible into Setswana. Both Makgothi and her father, Philip S. Mefare, were politically active—Makgothi was secretary of the Orange Free State branch of the South African Native National Congress, and Mefare was a member of its successor, the African National Congress. Kuzwayo began her schooling at a school built by Makgothi on his farm in Thabapatchoa, about 12 miles from Tweespruit, and attended Adams College, Amanzimtoti, before completing a teacher training course at Lovedale College in Fort Hare, graduating at age 22. She married Ernest Moloto in her late twenties, had two sons, and after enduring abuse, fled to Johannesburg. She had a part as a shebeen queen alongside Sidney Poitier in the 1951 film Cry, the Beloved Country. After her first marriage ended, she married Godfrey Kuzwayo in 1950. She taught in the Transvaal until 1952, when she gave up teaching due to the introduction of the Bantu Education Act, 1953, which limited black education opportunities. She then trained as a social worker from 1953 to 1955. After the 1976 Soweto uprising, she was the only woman on a committee of 10 tasked with organizing civic affairs in Soweto, and was detained for five months in 1977–78 under the Prevention of Terrorism Act; she later recounted her arrest in her 1996 testimony to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. She also served as president of the Black Consumer Union of South Africa and the Maggie Magaba Trust. In 1979, she was named Woman of the Year by The Star, and was nominated again in 1984. In 1987, she received an honorary doctorate of Laws from the University of the Witwatersrand, becoming the first black woman to receive such an honor from the university, and also received honorary doctorates from the University of Natal and the University of Port Elizabeth. She was awarded the Order of Meritorious Service by Nelson Mandela in 1999. With director Betty Wolpert, she co-produced the documentary films Awake from Mourning (1982) and Tsiamelo –– A Place of Goodness (1983), based on the story of her family's land dispossession. Kuzwayo died in Johannesburg at the age of 91 from complications of diabetes, survived by her sons Bobo and Justice Moloto, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. A South African marine research ship, the Ellen Khuzwayo, was named after her and launched in 2007.
